cases.quote: ’ 2019 RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK 右シングル引用符，右シングルクォーテーションマーク used in horizontal composition 横組で使用
cases.rationale: The first row of §A.2, quoted in the document's own column order — Character, UCS, Name, Common name, Remarks. Exactly three of §A.2's sixteen Remarks cells state anything and all three state a writing mode; this is one of them. A writing mode is not a frame (字幅) and not a role, and no cell anywhere in §A.2's Remarks column states a width, so nothing in this table separates this listing from §A.27's, which names 2019 with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」. The declared frame does: this occurrence is set on the ideographic frame, which §A.27's qualification does not describe, so cl-02 is what remains. The case declares no writing direction on purpose. §3.1.1's closing Note says that opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and hyphens (cl-03) use the same letter face in both writing modes, rotated 90 degrees clockwise to the inline direction, so nothing about a cl-02 occurrence's class turns on the mode: the Remarks cell restricts where the writing system uses this member, never which class it is in.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, first row, against §A.27's Remarks column (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27 lists 2019 with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」. This occurrence declares the ideographic frame, so the qualified listing does not describe it. §3.9.1 asks "Is the character width full-width, half-width, or something else?" / 「文字・記号の字幅は，全角か，半角か，又はそれ以外か．」 first among the axes on which positioning differs.

cases.quote: ” 201D RIGHT DOUBLE QUOTATION MARK 右ダブル引用符，右ダブルクォーテーションマーク used in horizontal composition 横組で使用
cases.rationale: The second row of §A.2, on the same input, because a case is one input and several questions about it. This row and the one above are the only place in §A.2 where the Remarks column over-states the document. §3.1.1's Note says of these two marks and their opening partners that they "are exclusively for horizontal writing mode and not to be used in vertical writing mode. However, in vertical writing mode, when Western characters (cl-27) are composed rotated 90 degrees clockwise, these quotation marks are sometimes used." The Remarks cell carries the prohibition and drops the exception, so a case written from the cell alone would publish a restriction the document does not make, and the exception is conditional on a rotation policy the caller owns rather than on anything §A.2 states. None of it changes the class of this occurrence: on the ideographic frame the answer is cl-02, and the case below supplies the rotated-Western occurrence the exception is about.

cases.quote: LEFT DOUBLE QUOTATION MARK "“" and RIGHT DOUBLE QUOTATION MARK "”" are exclusively for horizontal writing mode and not to be used in vertical writing mode. Also, LEFT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK "‘" and RIGHT SINGLE QUOTATION MARK "’" are exclusively for horizontal writing mode and not to be used in vertical writing mode. However, in vertical writing mode, when Western characters (cl-27) are composed rotated 90 degrees clockwise, these quotation marks are sometimes used.
cases.rationale: The same key as the case above on a different frame, and the answer is a different class. §A.27 lists 201D with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」, this occurrence declares exactly that frame, and §A.2's own cell says nothing about width — its qualification is a writing mode, which is a different axis and never selects a class — so §A.27's is the listing that describes a proportionally-set occurrence and §A.2's is what remains for every other frame. The sentence quoted above is why this case matters beyond the mechanics: the document names cl-27 itself for the rotated occurrence, so the class it reaches on the proportional frame is the class its own exception names. The case declares no writing direction even so. The exception is stated for vertical composition, but a proportionally-set right double quotation mark inside a run of Western text is cl-27 in horizontal composition too, and the frame is what says so. The advance is the caller's measurement of a proportional glyph and is not what decides this: the frame is declared, never inferred from the advance (ADR 0002).

permitted.source: JLReq §A.27's Remarks column for 201D, with §3.1.1's rotated-Western Note (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: Answering cl-02 for every occurrence of 201D is answering from the code point rather than from the occurrence, and it discards the only thing §A.27's Remarks column says. An implementation that does this cannot tell this case from `A.2/right-double-quotation-mark/second-occurrence`, and the two are one key on two frames.

cases.quote: For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: §A.2 keys its third row by 0029 and prints ）, U+FF09 FULLWIDTH RIGHT PARENTHESIS, in its own Character column; §3.9.2 illustrates the class as 「’”）〕］｝〉》」』】 など」, whose third, fifth and sixth glyphs are U+FF09, U+FF3D and U+FF5D — the compatibility forms and not the keys. The preamble Note quoted above is what licenses reading the two spellings as one member, so folding the Wide decomposition onto the key is required by the document rather than adopted for convenience. U+0029 is then the hardest key in the class: four Appendix A tables name it — §A.2, §A.25, §A.27 and §A.29 — and three of those four Remarks cells are empty, so the Remarks column is not what separates them. §A.27's is the one qualified cell, and the declared ideographic frame does not satisfy "proportionally-spaced". The other two listings are conditioned on a construct this input does not declare. §A.25 is 単位記号中の文字, characters *in* unit symbols, and §3.9.2 scopes it to "combinations of Latin script and Greek script characters used for international units (SI)" and adds a Note excluding full-width units in so many words: "There are units created with combinations of Latin and Greek script characters with a full-width character frame (full-width units). Such units are not part of the characters for units described here." §A.29 is conditioned on the bracket surrounding a warichu (割注), which the case below states. Neither condition holds here, so cl-02 is what remains.

permitted.source: JLReq §A preamble Note, with §3.9.2's own cl-02 example 「’”）〕］｝〉》」』】 など」

forbidden.why: §A.27 lists 0029 with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」, and this occurrence declares the ideographic frame. §3.9.2's own cl-27 Note states the axis: the Japanese and the Western parenthesis differ first in width, "Japanese, half em, Western, proportional".

§3.9.2 scopes cl-25 to "combinations of Latin script and Greek script characters used for international units (SI)" and its Note excludes full-width units from the class outright. This occurrence is on the ideographic frame and is in no unit symbol at all, so the §A.25 listing does not describe it.

§3.9.2's cl-29 Note says warichu brackets "are used for surrounding inline cutting notes and the space" and are a separate class because they "differ from normal brackets with regard to their processing". This input declares no warichu (割注), so the occurrence is one of the normal brackets that Note contrasts them with.

cases.quote: For example, LEFT PARENTHESIS "(" and RIGHT PARENTHESIS ")" has not only different width (Japanese, half em, Western, proportional) but are also different in line position (Japanese, center of the character frame in the inline direction, Western, base line and descender line dependent) and design (Japanese, slightly bent and constant line thickness, Western, strongly curved and dynamic line thickness).
cases.rationale: The same key as the case above on a different frame, and the answer is a different class — which is the whole reason a class is a function of an occurrence and not of a code point. The sentence quoted above is §3.9.2's own note on cl-27 and it names this very pair of code points, listing width first among the things that differ. §A.27 lists 0029 with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced", this occurrence declares that frame, and §A.2's row says nothing about width, so §A.27's is the listing that speaks about it. The advance is the caller's measurement of a proportional glyph and is not what decides this: the frame is declared, never inferred, and a proportional glyph exactly one em wide would be undecidable if it were (ADR 0002). §A.25 and §A.29 stay out for the reason the case above gives — the input declares no unit symbol and no warichu — and the frame does not reach them, because both of their Remarks cells for this key are empty.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.27's Remarks column for 0029, with §3.9.2's cl-27 Note (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.2's row for 0029 has an empty Remarks cell and therefore says nothing about width; §A.27's says "proportionally-spaced". Answering cl-02 on the proportional frame reads the unqualified listing over the qualified one, which reverses the only axis Appendix A gives for separating them.

cases.quote: warichu opening brackets (cl-28) and warichu closing brackets (cl-29) are used for surrounding inline cutting notes and the space. They are in a separate class since they differ from normal brackets with regard to their processing.
cases.rationale: §A.29 enumerates exactly three keys — 0029, 3015 and 005D — and every one of them is also a §A.2 key. Their §A.29 Remarks cells are empty and so are their §A.2 cells, so for these three no frame, no writing direction and no role separates the two listings; only the construct does, and the Note quoted above is where the document says so. A warichu closing bracket is a bracket that surrounds an inline cutting note (割注, warichu). This occurrence surrounds nothing, because the input declares no construct, so it is one of the "normal brackets" the Note contrasts them with and the answer is cl-02. An implementation that answered cl-29 from the code point would make every ordinary right square bracket in Japanese text a warichu bracket and would then read §3.4's warichu rules over text that has no warichu in it. The spelling is the compatibility one: §A.2 keys this row by 005D and prints ］, U+FF3D FULLWIDTH RIGHT SQUARE BRACKET, in its own Character column, so the Wide decomposition has to be folded before the table is consulted.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2 fifth row, against §A.29's three rows and §3.9.2's cl-29 Note (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.29 lists 005D with an empty Remarks cell, exactly as §A.2 does, so nothing an occurrence can declare about width, direction or role tells the two listings apart. What tells them apart is the warichu, and this input has none.

§A.27 lists 005D with the Remarks cell "proportionally-spaced". This occurrence declares the ideographic frame and carries the full-width compatibility spelling U+FF3D, which is the spelling the preamble Note says Japanese layout software uses.

cases.quote: LEFT TORTOISE SHELL BRACKET "〔" and RIGHT TORTOISE SHELL BRACKET "〕" are vertical variants of LEFT SQUARE BRACKET "［" and RIGHT SQUARE BRACKET "］", which are used in horizontal writing mode. Square brackets should be used in horizontal writing mode except for special cases.
cases.rationale: The fourth row of §A.2. Its Remarks cell is empty and so is the fifth row's, and the sentence quoted above is the only thing the document says about the two of them together. It is a recommendation about which member to choose — "should be used ... except for special cases" — and not a restriction on either member's usage, which is why neither cell says anything: both members are used in both writing modes, and 〕 in horizontal composition is a special case rather than an error. This is the exact mirror of the first two rows of the table. There the Remarks column over-states a direction fact and §3.1.1 refines it; here the Remarks column under-states one and §3.1.1 supplies it. Neither changes a class, and the case therefore declares no direction and expects cl-02 in both — which is what makes the recommendation observable as something an implementation must not act on, since an implementation that read it as a rule would have to answer something other than cl-02 for 〕 in horizontal composition and the document names no such class. 3015 is a §A.29 key as well, and it stays out for the reason `A.2/right-square-bracket/outside-a-warichu` gives.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, fourth row, with §3.1.1's statement about the pair (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.29's second row is 3015 with an empty Remarks cell. Only the warichu (割注) separates that listing from §A.2's, and this input declares no construct.

cases.quote: Among opening brackets (cl-01) and closing brackets (cl-02), LEFT PARENTHESIS "(", RIGHT PARENTHESIS ")", LEFT ANGLE BRACKET "〈" and RIGHT ANGLE BRACKET "〉" are used to indicate supplementary explanations, and in that case their usage differs slightly from other opening brackets (cl-01) and closing brackets (cl-02). To reflect the difference, there is an alternative convention to not append half em spacing before or after the parentheses and angle brackets, and instead just set them solid (see Figure 65).
cases.rationale: U+3009 and U+0029 are the two closing brackets §3.1.2's second Note singles out, and this case says exactly what does not depend on it. What the Note states is an alternative about spacing — whether the half em after the bracket is appended or the pair is set solid — and it does not state an alternative about class: §A.2 lists 3009 once, with an empty Remarks cell, no other Appendix A table names the key, and the Note's own words are that "their usage differs slightly", not that they belong somewhere else. So the answer is cl-02 under either convention and the case carries one permitted entry honestly. The alternative itself has no home in the suite yet, which is the reason this case exists rather than a pair: spec/derived/questions.tsv holds twenty policy questions and none of them is §3.1.2's, so a case pairing the two spacings with the policies that select them cannot be written today, and one written with a single permitted entry would turn a stated alternative into a requirement — which is the one thing this format exists to prevent. The quote is the English rendering of the Note deliberately. Its Japanese half names this member's glyph 〉 with the UCS name (LEFT ANGLE BRACKET), twice, where the correct name is RIGHT ANGLE BRACKET; the English half is right in both places and the glyph is right in both halves, so nothing about the class is affected, but a case quoting the Japanese half would publish a wrong UCS name.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, seventh row; §3.1.2's second Note states an alternative amount and no alternative class (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27's rows do not include 3009. The Note quoted above puts this member in cl-02 in the sentence that describes its special usage, so the usage cannot be read as taking it out of the class.

cases.quote: The following are lists of (non-ideographic) characters from a subset of ISO/IEC 10646 (collection number 285 "BASIC JAPANESE" and 286 "JAPANESE NON IDEOGRAPHICS EXTENSION") grouped by character class according to the classification explained in § 3.9.2 Grouping of Characters and Symbols depending on their Positioning.
cases.rationale: Nine of §A.2's sixteen keys are named by cl-02 and by no other Appendix A table — 2986, 3009, 300B, 300D, 300F, 3011, 3017, 3019 and 301F — and U+300D is the one ordinary Japanese prose uses most. On those nine there is no second listing for a frame, a role or a construct to select between, so the answer is the enumeration itself and nothing has to be disambiguated. The frame is declared all the same and may not be omitted, because cl-02 is one of the five classes whose advance §3.1.2 states, and there the frame decides a geometry rather than a class; the pair of cases below asserts that the class is the same on both of the frames that sentence names. The quoted preamble is also the boundary of the whole appendix and therefore of this class: the enumeration is closed against collections 285 and 286 of ISO/IEC 10646 rather than against Unicode, so a right-hand bracket Unicode encodes and those collections do not — U+2769 MEDIUM RIGHT PARENTHESIS ORNAMENT, U+27E7 MATHEMATICAL RIGHT WHITE SQUARE BRACKET, U+2E29 RIGHT DOUBLE PARENTHESIS — is outside the document's scope rather than excluded from cl-02. Neither the document nor this suite says what such a bracket is; §3.9.2 records that JIS X 4051 leaves an unmentioned character implementation-defined and that this document inherits the position.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, ninth row; no other Appendix A table lists 300D (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27's rows do not include 300D. A frame is what separates two listings of one key; it never creates a listing Appendix A does not have.

cases.quote: Note that breaking a line after opening brackets (cl-01) and before closing brackets (cl-02), full stops (cl-06) or commas (cl-07) is prohibited at all levels. Likewise, those rules common to all levels are not listed below.
cases.rationale: §C.3 lists four levels of kinsoku (禁則, line-break prohibition) convention and names cl-02 exactly once, in the sentence quoted above, whose content is that the prohibition around the class holds at every level. None of the four levels lists cl-02 among the classes or characters it relaxes. The contrast is §C.2 notes 1 to 3, the three places the document does say a character "shall be treated as a member of" another class: they name IDEOGRAPHIC ITERATION MARK, the prolonged sound mark (cl-10) and small kana (cl-11), and no cl-02 member. A closing bracket is therefore cl-02 at every level and under either reading of what a relaxation is, and the three entries below record that invariance across the whole relaxation surface rather than asserting it once. An implementation that discharged a level by moving classes around would change this occurrence's spacing and its answers against all six matrices, not only at the break the level was about.

permitted.source: JLReq §C.3's Strict level, which Policy::JLREQ selects; §A.2 decides the class (§3.9.2)
JLReq §C.3 level 1 "Very loose (Newspapers)" / 「レベル1（新聞など）」, whose list of relaxed classes does not name cl-02
The same level read as an override of Table 2's cell rather than as a reclassification (§C.3)

cases.quote: The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em). But when those punctuation marks are placed side-by-side with ideographic (cl-19), hiragana (cl-15), or katakana (cl-16) characters, in principle, a given amount of spacing will be inserted before or after the symbols, which makes them appear as if they were intrinsically full-width (one em).
cases.rationale: This case and the one below supply one key on the two frames the quoted sentence names, and expect the same class from both. cl-02 is one of the five classes on which a caller must declare a frame rather than may, and that sentence is why: on the ideographic frame the supplied advance already contains the amount that makes the bracket look full-width, and on the half-em frame it does not, so an unstated frame here leaves a geometry with no answer to report. What the frame decides for U+3011 is exactly that geometry and nothing else, because cl-02 is the only class Appendix A names it under and there is no second listing to select between. The two expectations are consequently identical, which is the assertion: an implementation that routes an item by the advance it was handed, rather than by the class the tables give it and the frame the caller declared, answers differently on the two halves of a pair that differ in nothing else.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, eleventh row, on the ideographic frame (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

cases.quote: 終わり括弧類（cl-02）では，原則として後ろを二分アキにする．
cases.rationale: The same member on the frame §3.1.2 says a closing bracket intrinsically has, with the advance a half-width body reports, and the same expected class. The quoted sentence is the per-class half of §3.1.2 — after a closing bracket, half em spacing is added in principle — and it is what the two frames are about: on this frame the amount is added to the caller's advance, and on the ideographic frame of the case above it is already inside it. The class does not move. §A.2's Remarks cell for 3011 is empty in both renderings, so the table states no width for this member and nothing in it prefers one frame; §A.27 does not list 3011, so no width-qualified listing competes with §A.2's either. An implementation that inferred a class from an advance — half-width therefore Western, full-width therefore Japanese — passes the case above and fails this one.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, eleventh row, on the half-em frame §3.1.2 describes (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: A half-width advance is not evidence of Western text. §A.27 does not list 3011 at all, and §3.1.2 states the half-width advance as the intrinsic one for every member of cl-02.

cases.quote: For example, while this document lists U+0028 LEFT PARENTHESIS as a member of opening brackets (cl-01), the compatibility counterpart U+FF08 FULLWIDTH LEFT PARENTHESIS is used in the Japanese context in most Japanese text layout software.
cases.rationale: §A.2's twelfth row keys U+2986 RIGHT WHITE PARENTHESIS and prints ｠, U+FF60 FULLWIDTH RIGHT WHITE PARENTHESIS, in its Character column — the same two-spelling arrangement as its third row, which keys U+0029 and prints ）. The two rows differ in one respect that decides whether an implementation gets this one right, and it is why this member has a case of its own. The usual shortcut for the halfwidth and fullwidth forms is arithmetic: subtract U+FEE0 from a code point in U+FF01 through U+FF5E. It covers ）, ］ and ｝, and it stops two code points short of ｠. U+FF5F and U+FF60 are the fullwidth white parentheses and their keys are U+2985 and U+2986, some four thousand code points below where the subtraction lands; on U+FF60 it yields U+0080, a C1 control that no Appendix A table names. So the failure is not a wrong class but a silent absence of one, on a member that is otherwise unambiguous — U+2986 is named by cl-02 and by nothing else. The Wide decomposition the preamble Note requires is a table lookup, and this row is the one that says an offset will not do.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, twelfth row, read through the §A preamble Note (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.27 lists neither 2986 nor FF60. The white parentheses have no Western listing anywhere in Appendix A, so no frame can reach one.

cases.quote: 〟 301F LOW DOUBLE PRIME QUOTATION MARK 終わりダブルミニュート used in vertical composition 縦組で使用
cases.rationale: The last row of §A.2 and the third of its three non-empty Remarks cells. §3.1.1 states the same restriction in prose and states it without an exception — "Though REVERSED DOUBLE PRIME QUOTATION MARK "〝" and LOW DOUBLE PRIME QUOTATION MARK "〟" are similar to double quotation marks in appearance they are exclusively used for vertical writing mode and are not to be used in horizontal writing mode" — which is what distinguishes this cell from the two horizontal-composition cells at the head of the table, where §3.1.1 does add one. U+301F is named by cl-02 and by no other Appendix A table, so no axis is consulted and the answer is the enumeration. The case declares no writing direction even so, and that is the claim worth publishing: a writing-mode restriction says where the writing system uses a member, not what class it is in, so a caller who composed 〟 horizontally — by mistake, or in a document about typography, or in a quotation of this very sentence — must still be told cl-02 and must be told the usage is wrong by some other answer than silence. Its opening partner U+301D is cl-01, so the pair spans two classes; nothing in §A.2 records that the two are a pair, and nothing here needs to.

forbidden.why: §A.27's rows do not include 301F. §3.1.1 says 〟 is "similar to double quotation marks in appearance" and Figure 62 shows it, but a resemblance is not a listing, and the two marks §A.27 does list — 2019 and 201D — are the ones §A.2 restricts to horizontal composition.

cases.quote: During layout processing, the issues mentioned in the previous section are addressed by grouping characters and symbols according to their characteristics, and handling them as character classes.
cases.rationale: §A.2 enumerates sixteen rows and every one of them keys a single code point, so cl-02 holds no code-point sequence at all and no row is duplicated. That is not true of Appendix A as a whole: §A.27 lists <02E5, 02E9> and <02E9, 02E5> as two distinct members, so the key of the appendix is an ordered sequence and a longest-first match over it is required — and over cl-02 that match has nothing to join. Two closing brackets written side by side are consequently two occurrences of two keys, and this case asks about the second one, which is the occurrence an implementation that glued the pair into one key would no longer have. Nothing in §A.2 says anything about what precedes a member, so the answer is the same as if it stood alone. The adjacency is also the commonest one the class has, since §3.1.4 exists to state the spacing where closing brackets follow one another, so an implementation that lost the second item would lose it in ordinary text and would be off by one in every count downstream.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.2, rows four and thirteen; sixteen single-code-point keys and no sequence (§3.9.2)

cases.quote: In JIS X 4051, IDEOGRAPHIC COMMA "、" and COMMA "," are classified as closing brackets (cl-02), because they have similar positioning methods. However, in this document, the handling of IDEOGRAPHIC COMMA "、" and COMMA "," are described as an independent class, named commas (cl-07).
cases.rationale: This is the boundary the document draws around cl-02 in its own words, in a Note attached to the cl-02 entry of §3.9.2 itself, and it is the single largest interoperability trap in the class. JIS X 4051 is the standard most Japanese layout code descends from; the positioning is close enough that the Note has to explain why the classes are not; and U+3001 is named by exactly one Appendix A table — §A.7, whose first row it is, with an empty Remarks cell — so an implementation answering cl-02 here is not resolving an ambiguity but contradicting the enumeration. The consequence is measurable at a boundary rather than only in a report: §B.2 note 5 records that under JIS X 4051, where a comma is followed by a middle dot (cl-05), the spacing between them is just the middle dot's quarter em, precisely because the comma is a closing bracket there. The item declares a frame because cl-07 is one of §3.1.2's five classes as well, and the frame it declares is the ideographic one, on which §A.7's unqualified row is the listing that describes it.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.7, first row, with §3.9.2's cl-02 Note (§3.9.2)

forbidden.why: §A.2's sixteen rows do not include 3001 and §A.7's first row is it. The Note quoted above names the other standard that does classify it as a closing bracket and says this document does not, so cl-02 here is not a permitted alternative but the reading the document set out to displace.

cases.quote: In JIS X 4051, IDEOGRAPHIC COMMA "、" and COMMA "," are classified as closing brackets (cl-02), because they have similar positioning methods. However, in this document, the handling of IDEOGRAPHIC COMMA "、" and COMMA "," are described as an independent class, named commas (cl-07).
cases.rationale: The other half of the same Note, and the harder half, because U+002C is named by three Appendix A tables where U+3001 is named by one. Two of the three qualify their listing on the frame: §A.24 gives it "quarter em width or half-width" / 「位取りのコンマ字幅は四分角又は半角」 and §A.27 gives it "proportionally-spaced" / 「プロポーショナル」. Neither describes an occurrence set on the ideographic frame, so §A.7's row is the listing that speaks — its own Remarks cell says only "used in horizontal composition" / 「横組で使用」, which is a writing mode and not a width — and the answer is cl-07 exactly as for the ideographic comma. cl-02 is not among the three tables at all, on any frame. The spelling is the compatibility one that §A.7's own Character column prints for this key, ，, U+FF0C FULLWIDTH COMMA, which is the form the convention §3.1.1 calls (i) and (ii) actually sets in horizontal Japanese text.

permitted.source: JLReq §A.7, second row, against §A.24's and §A.27's frame qualifications (§3.9.1, §3.9.2)

forbidden.why: No Appendix A table lists 002C under cl-02. §3.9.2's cl-02 Note names JIS X 4051 as the standard that does and says this document makes it cl-07 instead, so an implementation ported from a JIS X 4051 codebase fails here and nowhere it would notice.
